content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors consider the partial labels learning problem in the context of active learning. They introduce a concept counter-examples (CE) in human reasoning to propose the inverse RC loss (IRC). This CE method can help solve overfitting problem with enriching the input data. In order to make the loss better benefit both sample selection and predictor, they propose to enlarge the gap between the WorseNet (w) and Predictor (f) by adding the KLD regularization to the IRC to build the Worse loss. In empirical results, it shows that the WorseNet-based methods can improve the prediction accuracy in comparison with four active learning benchmark methods using five real word datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1.	The work explores a novel problem in active learning.
2.	The proposed WorseNet method can help improve the model prediction

Weakness:
1.	In the partial labels learning paper [Ref. 1], they propose the RC loss and guarantee the loss has theoretical support, such as convergence. However, there lacks of theoretical properties on the proposed IRC loss in this manuscript.

2.	Is the IRC loss and the KL divergence in the same scale? Why not add a tuning parameter before the KLD regularization?

3.	The two strategies to generate the partial labels may have issues. In Figure 1, the authors give a good example of when partial labeling is well justified: a wolf and a dog. It is hard for an imperfect agent to differentiate a wolf and a dog, because they are similar. However, the two strategies do not actually take this label similarity into account. For example, in the MNIST dataset, we know 1 and 7 might be hard to distinguish due to the similarity but 1 and 8 are different. Cases such as 1 and 8 will make the task easier than the real-world application. I think considering the similarity of the partial labels would make a more reasonable problem setup. (In some datasets, they do have hieratical labels which captures the similarity that can be used for more realistic partial labeling) 

4.	The empirical results for dataset SVHN, CIFAR-10, Lost, MSRCV2, and Yahoo!News do not make sense. The accuracy is too low, only around 25% accuracy. To convince the readers that the method is useful, it should at least get to an accuracy level that are acceptable by common sense, e.g. 60%, otherwise people will consider that either the model does not work or the evaluation setup is wrong. 

5.	A minor comment is that how the authors make the WorseNet better solve the overfitting problem than the others.

[Ref. 1] Feng, Lei, et al. "Provably consistent partial-label learning." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 10948-10960.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow. But there are a few points need clarification
1.	Why is the abbreviation of the minimum confidence uncertainty MCM?
2.	In Figure 3, the authors do not explain clearly why the selected points are more representative. For example, more points located around margins?

Quality
I think the story is complete, but there is no theoretical support for the idea. Also, I have some concerns about the empirical results. See weakness 4.

Novelty

The partial labeling problem is not novel, but it is new in active learning.

Reproducibility 

The author has provided a clear algorithm, so it should be easy to implement, but some parameters are unclear, such as the number of data points labeled by active learning for the result in Table 1 and what are the neural network configurations.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper needs to clarify the concerns the reviewer mentioned above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an augmentation method to train a complementary network for better partial label learning and better partial label active sample selection. The proposed method is inspired and designed according to the intuition of human counter-example learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper attempts to approach a practical and significant problem, which is the noisy human annotators in active learning.
2. The paper tries to develop the core method from human cognition study, which is innovative. A thorough and serious interdisciplinary study should always be encouraged. 
Weakness:
1. The proposed method lacks of novelty. The study of partial learning and usage of RC loss for training are directly borrowed from other work but they consist of a large portion of the paper content.
2. The challenge of the proposed problem is not well-posted. The only thing that the proposed worse net aims to solve is the overfitting of AL, which is a general problem for active learning. What about the active sampling challenge particularly for partial label prediction?
3. The proposed worsenet w  seems neither significant nor effective to me. Substituting eq 7 with eq6 the loss for training worsenet goes back to eq5. Then how could we understand the effectiveness of this additional classifier? And how it is different from f?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The explanation of the worsenet in terms of its effectiveness for training and active sampling remains at the intuition level. What is more, I don’t think partial labeling is a good model for active learning with noisy annotators. First, it is hard for an annotator to decide which label he/she wants to include. Second, it is hard to meet the assumption that the true label is included in the annotation set. The annotator might add many labels that he/she is not very certain about just because he/she wants to include the right label in the set. This might lead to a trivial annotation set(including all labels) in the end.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method lacks theoretical underpinning and novelty. The specific challenge of the proposed partial label active learning remains unclear in the end.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces the first-ever approach to active learning with partial labels (ALPL). It properly motivates both the task and the proposed approach, and it introduces the idea of learning from both examples and counter-examples. Finally, the paper introduces three ALPL algorithms and it performs a comprehensive empirical evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper introduces a the first approach to active learning with partial labels. It is well written and organized, and reasonably easy to follow. Overall, the idea of leveraging counter-examples to improve both prediction and selection makes intuitive sense, and the paper shows empirically that it also makes a difference in practice.

The paper could be further improved in two ways. First, it would benefit from a stand-alone section that would intuitively present an end-2-end running examples. Most of the information is already available in the paper, but, unfortunately, it is sprinkled in bits & pieces among the various section. Adding such a new section right after the introduction would greatly improve the paper's readability (and accessibility to readers unfamiliar with the domain). Second, the "Experiments" could be further improved by (i) explaining the setup for Tables 1 &2; right now, the reader must go to Fig 4 to see that the algorithms start with 20 partially-labeled examples and then query 980 more, (ii) for both Table 1 & 2, there should be an additional row that shows the best-achievable performance when training on all available data [rather than only 1000 examples], thus clarifying the approach's significance and impact, and (iii) a more insightful discussion about the results in tables 1 & 2 (see below).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper propose a novel idea, and it is well-written and organized. 

One way to improve its quality is to provide additional insight wrt to the results in tables 1 & 2. 
For example, the paper should emphasize that, overall, the idea of supplementing the learning process by leveraging counter examples makes both practical and intuitive sense (both for prediction and selection). Second, the paper should discuss why WS-MMU and WS-EU perform better than WS-MCM on the benchmark datasets, but worse in the real-world ones. Third, the paper should also offer insights into why, often times, all three WS-X algorithms, when used without WP," performs worse than random selection (eg, on Lost, MSRCV2, Yahoo,;
also, in Table 1, often times, one of the WS-X w/o WP also does worse than RS).  Overall, both Tables 1 & 2 should be simplified to better drive home a few crisp messages.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a well-written paper that, for an important topic (learning with partial labels), proposes a novel and impactful approach to active learning.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a setting for active learning, active learning with partial labels (ALPL), where a predictor trained on initial training examples annotated with partial labels. To address this problem, RC loss, a strong PLL baseline, is adapted for training the predictor. Furthermore, the paper exploits counter examples (CEs) sent to the proposed WorseNet to improve the predictor and selector in ALPL.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper studies a practical setting, which alleviates the annotation pressure in Active Learning.
2. The paper is overall clear, and the experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Weakness:
1. Some important references should be cited and discussed. One of the significant contributions in this paper is that it proposes a concept “counter examples” and then trains the WorseNet with them. However, complementary labels [1, 2] seem to have a lot of similarities with the labels of the counter labels, which needs some explanations to distinguish them. 

2. Some details are suggested to be further explained. “noise-tolerant partial labels”(In Page 2, line 11) , and “fake true label”(In Page 5, above Eq.(7)) are mentioned but are very confusing.

3. Figure 3 could be polished up. It seems that the left (EU, baseline) and the right (WS-EU, the proposed approach) does not have obvious differences. Part details of it are supposed to be highlighted, otherwise the figure does not make sense.

4. In Table 2, 8 and 9, it is confusing that the results of the baslines LL4AL, VAAL, and TA-VAAL are not presented but no explanation is made. 

5. The inverse RC loss in Eq.(7) is somewhat heuristic and rough, which needs more details to explain its reasonability.


[1] Ishida T, Niu G, Hu W, et al. Learning from complementary labels[J]. Advances in neural information processing systems, 2017, 30.
[2] Feng L, Kaneko T, Han B, et al. Learning with multiple complementary labels[C]. International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020: 3072-3081.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall problem setting and the proposed approaches are easy to understand but part of the important details, experimental results, and references need to be supplied to further clarify this paper. The problem setting is new in the community of Active Learning.  From part of the experimental results, the proposed approaches are effective. Since the approaches are not difficult, the reproducibility could be ensured.
content.summary_of_the_review: Some explanations need to be made to convince me. Therefore, at this stage, I will vote for borderline reject. The score could be re-evaluated based on the authors' responses.

content.title: Active Learning with Partial Labels
content.TL;DR: we propose a new problem setting named active learning with partial labels, where the oracle provides partial labels to the selected samples.
content.abstract: In this paper, we for the first time study a new problem setting called active learning with partial labels (ALPL), where an oracle provides the query samples with a set of candidate labels that contains the true label. Such a setting relaxes the oracle from the demanding labeling process. To address ALPL, we firstly propose a firm and intuitive baseline by directly adapting a state-of-the-art method for learning with partial labels to train the predictor, which can be seamlessly incorporated into existing AL frameworks. Inspired by human inference in cognitive science, we propose to improve the baseline by exploiting and exploring counter examples (CEs) to relieve the overfitting caused by a few training samples in ALPL. Specifically, we propose to construct CEs by reversing the partial labels for each instance, learning from which we propose a simple but effective WorseNet. By leveraging the distribution gap between WorseNet and the predictor, both the predictor itself and the sample selection process can be improved. Experimental results on five real-world datasets and four benchmark datasets show that our proposed methods achieve comprehensive improvements over ten representative AL frameworks, highlighting the superiority and effectiveness of CEs and WorseNet.
